summary:
Plant and animal tissues are different because of their structure and function. Plant cells have a cell wall that provides rigidity and strength, which helps them stay firm and upright in one place. This is unlike animal cells, which can change shape easily due to the lack of a rigid cell wall.

In plants, there are two types of meristematic tissues: apical meristem and lateral meristem. Apical meristem is responsible for growth in length, while lateral meristem is involved in growth in girth. The activity of these tissues helps plants grow in different ways - they increase in length (height of stem and depth of roots), increase in girth (thickness of stem), and regrow after cutting branches or grazing by animals.

The growth patterns in plants are influenced by the structure and function of their tissues. For example, plant roots grow only from the tips, whereas animal roots can grow throughout their entire length. This is why some plants have a single type of tissue that performs different functions, while others have multiple types of tissues that work together to achieve specific goals.

In animals, there are also different types of meristematic tissues, such as muscle and nervous tissue. Muscle tissue enables movement, while nervous tissue carries messages to different parts of the body. The division of labour in multicellular organisms is correlated with their structure and function, which helps them carry out complex life processes efficiently.

The study of cells and tissues is significant for understanding human welfare because it helps us understand how living organisms grow and develop. Tissues are groups of similar cells that work together to perform specific functions, and the division of labour at various levels of organisation in multicellular organisms is correlated with their structure and function. This knowledge can be applied to improve our daily lives by developing new technologies and treatments for diseases.
